items.readable_text:
Content:
Of particular importance in mathematical proofs are so-called biconditional statements. These are statements of the form

Content:
[MATH: (P\Rightarrow Q) \land (Q\Rightarrow P).]

Content:
In words, a biconditional statement states that "[MATH: P] implies [MATH: Q,] and [MATH: Q] implies [MATH: P.]"

Content:
Let's construct a truth table for this biconditional statement.

Content:
| [MATH: \,P\,] | [MATH: \,Q\,] | [MATH: \,P\Rightarrow Q\,] | [MATH: \,Q\Rightarrow P\,] | [MATH: \,(P \Rightarrow Q)\land (Q \Rightarrow P)\,] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] |

Content:
Biconditional statements are so important that we give them a special symbol.

Content:
[MATH: P\Leftrightarrow Q]

Content:
So, we now have the following logical equivalence:

Content:
[MATH: P \Leftrightarrow Q \equiv (P \Rightarrow Q) \land (Q \Rightarrow P)]

Content:
The truth table for [MATH: P\Leftrightarrow Q] is as follows:

Content:
| [MATH: \,P\,] | [MATH: \,Q\,] | [MATH: \,P\Leftrightarrow Q\,] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] |

Content:
According to the truth table, [MATH: P\Leftrightarrow Q] is true if [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] have the same truth value. Otherwise, it is false. We can express this as another logical equivalence:

Content:
[MATH: P\Leftrightarrow Q \equiv \big(P \land Q\big) \lor \big(\neg P \land \neg Q\big)]

Content:
There are many ways to say [MATH: P\Leftrightarrow Q] in words. Among the most common are the following:

Content:
- [MATH: P] is equivalent to [MATH: Q]
- [MATH: P] if and only if [MATH: Q]
- If [MATH: P] then [MATH: Q,] and if [MATH: Q] then [MATH: P]
- [MATH: P] implies [MATH: Q], and [MATH: Q] implies [MATH: P]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
According to the definition of the biconditional,

  • [MATH: A \Leftrightarrow B] is true if [MATH: A\Rightarrow B] and [MATH: B\Rightarrow A.] Otherwise, it is false.

  • In other words, [MATH: A \Leftrightarrow B] is true if [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] have the same truth values. Otherwise, it is false.

So, when [MATH: A = \textrm T] and [MATH: B = \textrm T,] we have [MATH: (A⇔B)|= (T⇔T); = T.]

The complete truth table is shown below:

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Of particular importance in mathematical proofs are so-called biconditional statements. These are statements of the form

Content:
[MATH: (P\Rightarrow Q) \land (Q\Rightarrow P).]

Content:
In words, a biconditional statement states that "[MATH: P] implies [MATH: Q,] and [MATH: Q] implies [MATH: P.]"

Content:
Let's construct a truth table for this biconditional statement.

Content:
| [MATH: \,P\,] | [MATH: \,Q\,] | [MATH: \,P\Rightarrow Q\,] | [MATH: \,Q\Rightarrow P\,] | [MATH: \,(P \Rightarrow Q)\land (Q \Rightarrow P)\,] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] |

Content:
Biconditional statements are so important that we give them a special symbol.

Content:
[MATH: P\Leftrightarrow Q]

Content:
So, we now have the following logical equivalence:

Content:
[MATH: P \Leftrightarrow Q \equiv (P \Rightarrow Q) \land (Q \Rightarrow P)]

Content:
The truth table for [MATH: P\Leftrightarrow Q] is as follows:

Content:
| [MATH: \,P\,] | [MATH: \,Q\,] | [MATH: \,P\Leftrightarrow Q\,] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm T] |
| [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] | [MATH: \textrm F] |
| [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm F] | [MATH: \textrm T] |

Content:
According to the truth table, [MATH: P\Leftrightarrow Q] is true if [MATH: P] and [MATH: Q] have the same truth value. Otherwise, it is false. We can express this as another logical equivalence:

Content:
[MATH: P\Leftrightarrow Q \equiv \big(P \land Q\big) \lor \big(\neg P \land \neg Q\big)]

Content:
There are many ways to say [MATH: P\Leftrightarrow Q] in words. Among the most common are the following:

Content:
- [MATH: P] is equivalent to [MATH: Q]
- [MATH: P] if and only if [MATH: Q]
- If [MATH: P] then [MATH: Q,] and if [MATH: Q] then [MATH: P]
- [MATH: P] implies [MATH: Q], and [MATH: Q] implies [MATH: P]

---
